stories.title: July was third hottest month on record, says Met Éireann
stories.summary: New statistics show that last month was one of the hottest, driest and sunniest months on record for Ireland. According to Met Éireann's climate statement for last month, July 2026 was the second hottest July on record since 1900. The forecaster has said the month was dominated by high pressure, which resulted in a national mean July temperature of 17.25C. This has only ever been topped by the mean temperature for July 2013 of 17.34C.

stories.title: Brittany Ferries to cease live animal exports
stories.summary: Brittany Ferries will cease live animal exports to France from next month, a decision that has raised concern with the Irish Farmers Association (IFA). A spokesperson for the French shipping company confirmed the transport of live farm animals to France would end, but added that it would be making no further comment. IFA President Francie Gorman said he raised the issue with Minister for Agriculture Martin Heydon today. In a statement, he said it was "imperative" that Minister Heydon and his EU counterparts ensure Irish cattle "continue to have unhindered access" to the Single Market.

stories.title: Donald Trump set to travel to Doonbeg for Irish Open
stories.summary: US President Donald Trump is set to travel to Ireland next month for a visit that will include his attendance at the Irish Open at his golf course in Doonbeg, Co Clare, and events in Dublin. This date is to ensure he will be in the US for the annual commemoration of the 11 September terrorist attacks, and that he will be in Doonbeg in time for the end of the Irish Open on 13 September. Mr Trump's visit will also include a trip to Dublin, which is likely to involve a meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin. However, sources said it is highly unlikely that Mr Trump will give a speech to the Dáil or Seanad, or attend any events at Leinster House, as TDs and senators are not due to return from their summer break until 16 September.

stories.summary: Betting giant and Paddy Power owner Flutter Entertainment said today that company veteran and head of its international division Dan Taylor will succeed Peter Jackson as CEO later this year. Flutter said that Peter Jackson's nine years as group chief executive officer will come to an end on October 1. Dan Taylor most recently assumed the expanded role of Flutter president in May, with responsibility for overseeing the group's underperforming US operations following the departure of Amy Howe as head of its market-leading FanDuel brand. The company said that Mr Jackson will remain with Flutter as an advisor until the end of the year to support a smooth transition.

stories.title: Reed, MacIntyre, Molinari and Straka sign up for Doonbeg
stories.summary: Ryder Cup stars Patrick Reed, Robert MacIntyre, Francesco Molinari, and Sepp Straka have been confirmed for the 2026 Amgen Irish Open, with the quartet set to tee it up at Trump International Golf Links & Hotel from 10-13 September. They will join a field that already includes defending champion Rory McIlroy, two-time major champion and two-time Irish Open champion Jon Rahm, as well as major champions and former Open winners Shane Lowry and Pádraig Harrington. The field also features European Ryder Cup captain Luke Donald, alongside some of his squad members, Tyrrell Hatton, Rasmus Højgaard and Nicolai Højgaard. Rasmus was Irish Open champ at Royal County Down two years ago. Reed, the 2018 Masters champion, currently leads the Race to Dubai on the DP World with two victories, a runner-up finish and two further top-ten results this season.

stories.title: Manley: Cork overcame early-season doubts in 2026
stories.summary: Cork camogie manager Ger Manley admits the side overcame early-season doubts amid a big turnover in personnel to return to the All-Ireland final for the sixth year in succession. The Rebels' bid for a third All-Ireland title on the trot was ended in dramatic fashion, with a one-point loss to Galway last year, Carrie Dolan's free deciding the game in favour of the westerners, who they face again on Sunday. One of the game's most decisive moments was Hannah Looney's sending off shortly before half-time, which left the then champions hobbled for the remainder of the game. The high-profile midfielder was one of those Cork players to join the exodus in the off-season, joining Hawthorn in the AFLW. The Mackey sisters, Pamela and Katrina, also called it quits at the end of the 2025 season.

stories.title: Rovers boss Bradley warns Albanians are 'the best yet'
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers will look to keep alive their hopes of European group stage football as they take on KF Egnatia in the Europa League third round qualifying at Tallaght Stadium on Tuesday. The Hoops dropped down to the Europa League after a disappointing second-half performance at home saw them lose to Armenian side Ararat-Armenia in the Champions League qualifiers. Trailing 2-0 from the first leg in Armenia, Rovers produced a wonderful first 45 minutes in the second leg to level the tie up as 2-2 by half-time, but they were unable to build on that and a 73rd-minute goal by Brazilian striker Sandro Lima saw them drop down a tier. A win for Rovers would move them into the Europa League play-off round for a match against Lillestrom of Norway, a prize that also guarantees participation in the group stages of the Conference League.

stories.title: 10 must-see shows at Dublin Fringe Festival 2026
stories.summary: In her 2nd year as Dublin Fringe Festival Director, Bee Sparks highlights 10 must-see shows to consider for your festival diary this September. This is Dublin Fringe's boldest programme yet, a festival that takes over the city for 16 days and nights of exceptional, multidisciplinary work. This year the festival sets out to reignite our love affair with Dublin City, championing the irrepressible, indomitable creative force of Ireland’s artists and audiences, creating a festival that reflects the Ireland of today: the breadth of communities who call it home, the crucial conversations that shape our reality, and the visions that show us how things could be. Expect breath-taking performances across a sweeping spectrum of artforms - experience sharp new plays grappling with contemporary life - gas comedy to bring the belly-laughs - and interdisciplinary spectacle that forges new forms. stories.title: What does power dressing look like in 2026?
stories.summary: The words 'power dressing' immediately bring to mind sharp suits and big shoulders, but where does the concept originate from, and what does it look like for us today? Fashion historian Laura Fitzachary joined Doireann Garrihy to discuss the history of power dressing amongst the political class. Listen back above. Far from the sell-sell-sell power brokers of the 1980s, Fitzachary says that "if you're looking at it from a historical point of view, you could argue that it comes from the emergence of royal portraiture, court portraiture. That's where you really see people depicted in their finery, in a lot of detail." In this era, power was best signposted by the medium of painting, where one artist could be brought in to paint a subject's face and hands, while any amount of specialist painters would be brought in to depict the intricate clothing they wore, from lace and velvet to shining pearls.

stories.title: Ceuta crisis puts Ireland's EU presidency to the test
stories.summary: Of all the potential flashpoints that risked overshadowing the first weeks of Ireland's EU presidency, it is safe to say Ceuta was until recently not one. The tiny Spanish territory on the north African coastline has long been a source of dispute in the region. But with Aughinish Alumina, ongoing calls for a possible EU-wide version of the occupied territories bill, social media age restrictions and domestic political matters, only the best of predictors would have suggested the autonomous location just 18.5km in size was going to garner much attention. All of that changed this week when a sudden influx of Moroccan migrants into Ceuta pushed the area directly into an EU spotlight which is unlikely to dim any time soon.

stories.title: Next ups profit outlook again on warm weather sales boost

Shares in Next, which trades from more than 800 stores in the UK and Ireland and has an online operation serving the UK and overseas, rose 7% in early trade, extending their gain so far in 2026 to 19%. Next had forecast that second-quarter full-price sales growth would slow to 4% after growth of 6.2% in its first quarter, reflecting a tough comparative number in the same period last year. However, sales were £70m ahead of forecast in the 13 weeks to August 1 - £19m in the UK and £51m overseas.

stories.summary: Ukraine has expressed outrage over a video showing a man chased by a drone in Kherson city and denounced it as a deliberate "hunt" and "safari" targeting civilians. In the footage, which could not immediately be verified by AFP, a man seeks shelter behind a vehicle from a remotely piloted FPV (first-person view) drone pursuing him before detonating its explosive charge. The man, who was selling vegetables at a street market in the southern city, "suffered bodily injuries but survived", the head of Kherson City Military Administration, Yaroslav Shanko, said on Telegram. "I had only set up the umbrellas and began taking the crates out... My wife was there too. We heard a buzzing sound," the victim, a 52-year-old man identified as Yuriy, recounted in a video posted by local authorities.

stories.title: Trainor hoping to make Merry at last in Croker
stories.summary: The sense of renewed hope that comes with the commencement of each season is familiar to most of us that ever laced up a pair of boots, or follow a team. Players are not immune and it would be very hard for the majority to keep at it otherwise. There are various levels, of course, and getting so close but not getting over the line might be viewed by some as a first world issue. That said, it doesn't take a psychology degree to understand the price of being immersed in what at times of despair can seem a Sisyphean task. Of having hopes raised, of reaching final after final, and just not getting the job done. People talk of deserving in such instances. The word doesn’t exist in the lexicon of those that inhabit elite environments. But as Florence Welch memorably warbles, it’s always darkest before the dawn. And when the sun rises, it invariably brings with it a feeling of respair.

stories.title: Ospreys or Scarlets face axe as WRU outlines cut plans
stories.summary: Wales are to go ahead with plans to cut their number of professional franchises from four to three, spelling the end for either the Ospreys or Scarlets, both former winners of the United Rugby Championship. The Welsh Rugby Union on Wednesday confirmed the proposed change to the professional game and plans to establish three men's teams from the 2028/29 season – one based in the capital, one in west Wales and one in east Wales. Cardiff, owned by the Welsh Rugby Union, and Dragons, an independently backed business, are set to be given licences, leaving Swansea-based Ospreys and Llanelli-based Scarlets to compete for the remaining spot. Ospreys have won the URC, in its previous guise, four times, most recently in 2012.

stories.title: In the arena - John Healy's long road back from literary oblivion
stories.summary: Ahead of a special IFI screening of his acclaimed documentary Barbaric Genius, filmmaker Paul Duane reflects on the life and literary legacy of the film's subject, Grass Arena author John Healy. The first time I spoke to John Healy, over the phone in 2007, I remember feeling not quite frightened, but possibly intimidated, approaching him. This was a man with a legend around him, a man who had emerged from the underclass with an incendiary memoir telling stories not only of violence and squalor but also of great intellectual abilities that were rendered invisible by Healy's position as Irish and working-class in fifties Britain. A memoir that came dressed in the black and green hardback livery of Faber & Faber, but which emerged from the recognisable world of London's squares and squats, a London I recognised from my time spent there, seeing for the first time how the left-behind of the Irish diaspora existed in a state of desperation made bearable by whatever drugs and alcohol they could scrounge.

stories.title: Irish actor Jack Gleeson cast in new Poirot adaptation
stories.summary: Game of Thrones and House of Guinness star Jack Gleeson has joined the cast of a new BBC series based on Agatha Christie's detective Hercule Poirot. Other cast members include A Good Girl’s Guide To Murder actor Henry Ashton, James D’Arcy of Oppenheimer, Supacell’s Calvin Demba, Smoggie Queens actor Phil Dunning, The Buccaneers actor Guy Remmers, and Maggie actress Rebecca Rittenhouse. The new adaptation aims to show how the detective rose to prominence and is due to begin filming soon, primarily in Liverpool.

stories.title: How a 200-year-old building became a coffee shop made of scrap
stories.summary: Nestled in the bustling heart of Monaghan town, Genesis is a coffee shop with a difference. Not only is it built with community in mind, driving business into a previously derelict building, but it has been handmade using repurposed objects. The sturdy floor is made from old scaffold planks and repurposed tiles; the counter is made from "a bit of a shed"; tables were carved from items found in a skip; and light fittings in the ceiling are crafted from old sewing machines. "There were a few sewing machines in the building," explains Kevin, "so I kept a bit of that history there, and converted them into lights. I made two of them and got an electrician to connect them up." Having worked on building sites for many years, Kevin McGuire says he became pretty "handy" over the years, jokingly describing himself as a 'Jack of all trades, but master of none'.

stories.title: Nearly 6,000 contact HSE for help finding a GP this year
stories.summary: Almost 6,000 people have contacted the Health Service Executive already this year seeking help in finding a GP. New figures also indicate that while Ireland's population increased by around 10% between 2020 and 2025, the total number of GPs increased by just 6.4%, as population growth continues to outstrip growth in services, creating a deficit of doctors to meet patient needs. The number of GPs treating patients with medical cards has risen by just 2.3% between 2020 and 2025, although the number of GPs entering private practice has increased by 26.8%. Just 59 GPs have signed up to provide care under the General Medical Services (GMS) scheme for patients with medical cards and GP visit cards since 2020.

stories.title: Stage-four cancer survivor hails rehabilitation trial
stories.summary: A man who is in remission from stage-four prostate cancer has said he is "a different person" after taking part in a 12-week rehabilitation trial. The pioneering cancer rehabilitation trial in Cork has received renewed funding from the Irish Cancer Society, with researchers hoping it will help make supportive rehabilitation a routine part of cancer care in Ireland. Launched in 2022, the LIAM Mc Trial (Linking In with Advice and supports for Men with Metastatic Cancer) saw men living with advanced prostate, bladder and kidney cancers receive specialist physiotherapy, nursing, dietetic advice and psychological support twice weekly over 12 weeks. Developed by Cancer Research at UCC and supported by €300,000 in funding from the Irish Cancer Society, the programme saw 56 men take part, with researchers noting an "overwhelmingly positive response" from participants.

stories.title: Labour's Bev Craig elected mayor of Greater Manchester
stories.summary: The UK's ruling Labour Party comfortably retained the mayoralty of Greater Manchester following an election triggered by new Prime Minister Andy Burnham's return to parliament. Bev Craig, the leader of Manchester City Council, was elected after winning 47.15% of the votes in the first round. The anti-immigration Reform UK party, which had been riding high in national polls, came in second place with a 21% share. Without the 50% of votes needed to win outright, the counting proceeded to a second round.

stories.title: Heineken's first-half profit rises as 3,000 jobs cut
stories.summary: Heineken has today reported forecast-beating first-half profit after cutting about 3,000 jobs, roughly half of the up to 6,000 reductions targeted under a two-year restructuring plan. Former CEO Dolf van den Brink announced the cuts in February as the world's second-largest brewer sought to tackle weak beer demand across the industry. Heineken, which makes Tiger and Sol beer alongside its namesake lager, said it had made material progress on the plan, helping widen its operating margin. Chief Financial Officer Harold van den Broek said the cuts were "enterprise-wide" and resulted from initiatives across breweries, the supply chain, head office and individual markets, with Europe a "big component".

stories.title: Bradley disappointed Rovers didn't score more goals
stories.summary: Shamrock Rovers manager Stephen Bradley admitted to feeling frustrated despite his side's 3-1 victory over Albanian outfit Egnatia in the Europa League third qualifying round. A 29th-minute penalty by Graham Burke, converted after Dylan Watts had been brought down, handed the League of Ireland side the lead at Tallaght Stadium before the visitors levelled, Guillem Jaime scoring on the rebound after goalkeeper Ed McGinty had saved his penalty. Pico Lopes fired the Hoops back in front from Jack Byrne’s pass in the 56th minute before Aaron Greene netted two minutes later to put them in control ahead of the return leg in Albania. However, Rovers could and should have added to their lead as Burke, Jonathan Afolabi and Jake Mulraney all had big chances to cap off an impressive second-half display with further goals.

stories.summary: Waterford great Ken McGrath has joined Stephen Molumphy's Déise backroom team for the 2027 season. The Mount Sion player won four Munster SHC titles during a celebrated career between 1996 and 2011, picking up three All-Stars in the process. Shane Briggs has also joined Molumphy's backroom team, having spent last season with Carlow, while Nigel Skehan is retained from Peter Queally's management team.
